newsitem.title: JAPAN: Dollar's dive likely to be limited - Tokyo dealers.
newsitem.headline: Dollar's dive likely to be limited - Tokyo dealers.

text.p: Despite a nearly four-yen tumble on Friday, the dollar is unlikely to sink to the 110-yen level seen in May because of the strong fundamentals in the United States, dealers in Japan said on Monday.
But they added that moves in U.S. asset markets would be the key to the dollar's trend, and that another heavy selloff in U.S. stocks and bonds could put further pressure on the greenback.

"The latest drop in the dollar was basically due to position-adjustment sales after excessive longs were built up in recent trade... The situation is not the same as in May when the dollar experienced a freefall," said Katsunori Shiga, vice president at Chase Manhattan Bank in Tokyo.
He added that unlike the situation in May, when the dollar fell more than 15 yen within a month, there had been no significant attempt by Japanese monetary officials to halt the dollar's advance.
"No significant change in fundamental factors was detected behind the dollar's fall against the yen," Shiga said.

The dollar stood at around 115.05/10 yen in late-afternoon trade on Monday due to purchases by Japanese investors and U.S. fund operators. The rebound came after it hit a low of 114.25 yen in New York on Friday.
Dealers said relative strength in the U.S. economy and the poor outlook for Japan economy will underpin the dollar.

"I don't think the dollar will weaken to 110 yen soon. If you consider the current fundamentals (in Japan), you don't want to buy the yen aggressively either," said Toshiaki Enomoto, manager at Sanwa Bank.
But dealers said whether the dollar's fall would be short-lived or not would depend on moves in U.S. stocks and bonds.

"The key point (for currency markets) will be how far U.S. asset markets, such as stocks and bonds, will face further corrective sales in the future," said Nobuya Shida, manager of trading division at the Long-Term Credit Bank of Japan.
He added that the dollar's latest dip was still a corrective phase of the dollar/yen rate, but if U.S. stock markets collapsed after the recent strong rally, it would be another story for the dollar.
Dealers said they were focusing on U.S. data due out this week, including a retail sales report for July on Wednesday, for clues to U.S. asset markets.
Nobuo Kihara, head of foreign-exchange marketing at Banque Paribas in Tokyo said the dollar's decline against the yen may be more limited than against the mark.
He cited possible buying back of the mark against the yen in cross trade, which would indirectly support the dollar against the yen.
